title: Sleepy Hollow and Other American Halloween Stories
author: Washington Irving, Edgar Allan Poe and others
written: Between 1820 and 1926, by seven writers who had no October holiday in mind
setting: A Dutch valley on the Hudson, a Salem forest at night, a house beside a tarn, a Missouri cabin, a nursery with barred windows, and a castle with no stairs up
lengthNote: Twelve stories by seven writers, about 95,000 words, with notes returning each to the magazine or volume it first appeared in
openingLine: In the bosom of one of those spacious coves which indent the eastern shore of the Hudson, at that broad expansion of the river denominated by the ancient Dutch navigators the Tappan Zee, and where they always prudently shortened sail, and implored the protection of St. Nicholas when they crossed, there lies a small market town or rural port, which by some is called Greensburgh, but which is more generally and properly known by the name of Tarry Town.
summary: Twelve American stories that Halloween adopted afterwards. Irving's schoolmaster rides home past a Dutch burying ground; Hawthorne's Goodman Brown walks into the forest and comes back unable to look at his neighbours; Poe supplies a house, a cat and a heart under the floorboards; Bierce, Gilman and Freeman work the same ground colder; and Lovecraft's Outsider climbs out of a castle to find a mirror. Not one was written for the holiday, and the introduction follows how the holiday got them — through jack-o'-lanterns, print, repetition and trade.
referenceStyle: story title, with first publication given in the notes

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Legend of Sleepy Hollow (eBook 41)
sourceText.note: Irving's story as printed in The Sketch Book. The quotations here all come from it, the collection’s lead story; the other eleven are noted by title and first publication.

atAGlance.label: Twelve stories
atAGlance.note: From Irving's Sketch Book to Lovecraft's The Outsider, a century apart.

atAGlance.label: Seven writers
atAGlance.note: Irving, Hawthorne, Poe, Bierce, Gilman, Freeman and Lovecraft.

atAGlance.label: Not for Halloween
atAGlance.note: Every story predates the holiday's modern shape; the association was made later, by publishers and readers.

atAGlance.label: The apparatus
atAGlance.note: Each story is returned to its first printing, with a chronology of the holiday and a glossary.

structure.label: Washington Irving
structure.title: A Dutch valley, a schoolmaster and a bargain with the devil
structure.summary: The collection opens with the two Irving tales that taught American writing how to be funny and frightening in the same paragraph. Sleepy Hollow spends most of its length on food, dancing and local gossip before it puts anything on the road behind Ichabod; The Devil and Tom Walker is a New England money story with a black man in the swamp keeping the accounts.

scenes.title: The Hollow
scenes.summary: A valley where a drowsy influence hangs over the land, and where the local ghost is a Hessian trooper looking for his head.

scenes.title: The Van Tassel party
scenes.summary: Food, fiddling and war stories, and a schoolmaster refused by the heiress before he rides home.

scenes.title: The swamp
scenes.summary: A miserly Massachusetts man meets the devil among the ruins of an Indian fort and takes the usury business.

structure.label: Nathaniel Hawthorne
structure.title: Young Goodman Brown and The Minister’s Black Veil
structure.summary: Hawthorne makes the New England past a moral problem with no way out. Young Goodman Brown goes into the woods on one night's errand and never recovers from what he may only have dreamed; The Minister's Black Veil puts a piece of crape between one man and his parish and lets the parish supply the meaning.

scenes.title: The errand
scenes.summary: A night walk into the forest, a congregation at a fire, and a man who cannot afterwards look at his wife.

scenes.title: The crape
scenes.summary: A minister covers his face and refuses to explain, and the explanation his people invent is the story.

structure.label: Edgar Allan Poe
structure.title: Usher, The Black Cat and The Tell-Tale Heart
structure.summary: Three of the most quoted stories in American literature, all told by men explaining themselves. Usher is atmosphere and collapse; The Black Cat and The Tell-Tale Heart are confessions from narrators who begin by insisting on their sanity and end by producing the evidence against themselves.

scenes.ref: The Fall of the House of Usher (1839)
scenes.title: The tarn
scenes.summary: A visitor arrives at a house with a fissure in it, and leaves as the fissure finishes its work.

scenes.title: Under the boards
scenes.summary: A murder committed for an eye, and a sound the murderer alone can hear while the police sit talking.

scenes.title: The wall
scenes.summary: Drink, cruelty, a second cat, and a rap on the plaster that gives the whole thing away.

structure.label: Bierce, Gilman and Freeman
structure.title: Stories from the 1890s
structure.summary: Four stories from the 1890s and after, written by people who had seen a civil war and a rest cure. Bierce's horrors are reported flatly, by soldiers and coroners; Gilman's room is a medical arrangement; Freeman's haunting arrives as a domestic detail that the women of the house discuss over their work.

scenes.title: The cabin
scenes.summary: A frontier widower sits with his wife's body, and the reason the window is boarded is given in the last sentence.

scenes.title: The inquest
scenes.summary: A coroner's court hears about a creature of a colour outside human sight, and returns the verdict it prefers.

scenes.title: The room
scenes.summary: A rest cure, a barred nursery and a pattern with something behind it.

scenes.title: The shadow
scenes.summary: A shadow in a New England parlour that matches nobody present, and the sisters who keep looking at it.

structure.label: Lovecraft, and the holiday
structure.title: The Outsider, and how the stories became Halloween reading
structure.summary: Lovecraft’s story closes the century of writing the book covers, and the introduction then does the other half of the job: how jack-o’-lanterns, postcards, shop decorations and repeated anthologies made a set of unrelated tales into Halloween reading.

scenes.title: The mirror
scenes.summary: A climb out of a castle with no stairs up, a lit house, and a reflection.

scenes.title: Making the canon
scenes.summary: Trick-or-treating, printing and habit: how the stories acquired an October association none of their authors intended.

characters.name: Ichabod Crane
characters.role: The Connecticut schoolmaster of Sleepy Hollow
characters.summary: Lank, greedy, superstitious and calculating, he courts an heiress for her father's barns and reads Cotton Mather for pleasure after dark. Irving gives him no dignity and a good deal of sympathy, and then removes him from the story without saying what happened.
characters.clue: Has the dilating powers of an anaconda at a table, and an appetite for the marvellous to match.

relationships.label: pursued by, or believes he is

characters.name: Brom Bones
characters.role: Abraham Van Brunt, the local champion
characters.summary: Broad, good-humoured and fond of practical jokes, he is the obvious husband and the obvious suspect. Irving's last paragraphs let him look knowing whenever the pumpkin is mentioned, which is as close to a solution as the story offers.
characters.clue: Laughs whenever anyone brings up the pumpkin found beside the hat.

characters.name: Katrina Van Tassel
characters.role: The farmer's daughter, and his only heir
characters.summary: Eighteen, plump, and perfectly aware of what she is worth. She is described in the same sentences as her father's land and livestock, which is Irving's joke about the courtship and his most pointed observation about it.
characters.clue: Is appraised alongside the barns, the poultry and the buckwheat fields.

characters.name: The Headless Horseman
characters.role: The Hessian trooper of the local stories
characters.summary: A cavalryman whose head was carried off by a cannon-ball in the Revolution, said to ride nightly in search of it and to be obliged to return to the churchyard before daybreak. He exists in the village's talk long before he appears on the road, which is how Irving has it both ways.
characters.clue: Throws his head, and the head turns out to be a pumpkin.

characters.name: Young Goodman Brown
characters.role: Hawthorne's Salem husband, out for one night
characters.summary: He leaves his wife Faith at sunset on an errand he will not describe and meets, in the forest, everybody he has been taught to respect. Whether the meeting happened is left open; what it does to the rest of his life is not.
characters.clue: Comes home and will not take his wife's hand in the street.

characters.name: Poe's narrators
characters.role: The men explaining themselves in three of the stories
characters.summary: Each opens by disputing an accusation nobody in the text has made — that he is mad, or nervous, or fanciful — and then supplies the account that convicts him. Poe's method is to make the reader the jury and the confession the evidence.
characters.clue: Insists on his own sanity in the first paragraph, every time.

relationships.label: the other kind of American guilt

characters.name: The narrator of The Yellow Wall-Paper
characters.role: A woman under a rest cure, writing in secret
characters.summary: Forbidden to work, she gives the pattern on the wall the attention she would have given a book, and finds a woman behind it. The story is the sharpest thing in the volume about who is believed, and it was written by someone who had been through the treatment.
characters.clue: Keeps a journal because writing has been forbidden.

characters.name: The Outsider
characters.summary: He has lived in a castle among books and cannot remember anyone speaking to him. The story is a single movement upward towards light and company, and its last paragraph rearranges everything that came before it.
characters.clue: Reaches for the figure in the doorway and touches a mirror.

themes.name: Village superstition
themes.summary: The collection's hundred years runs from a community's shared ghost to a single mind's private one. Irving's horseman belongs to everyone in the Hollow; Poe's heart is audible to one man; Gilman's woman is behind one room's paper.
themes.development: The fear moves steadily indoors and inward, and the later stories have no village left to consult.

themes.name: Narrators
themes.summary: Nearly every story arrives through a teller with an interest: a chronicler quoting a village, a murderer insisting on his sanity, a coroner's court reading from a dead man's diary, a woman writing where she has been told not to.
themes.development: Irving's narrator is amused and detached; by the 1890s the tellers are inside the events, and by The Outsider the teller does not know what he is.

themes.name: Concealment
themes.summary: Hawthorne’s veil, Poe’s floorboards and plastered wall, Bierce’s boarded window: again and again the volume hides something and then listens to it. Concealment is the plot of at least half these stories.
themes.development: In Hawthorne the guilt is general and unnameable; in Poe it is specific and buried; in Bierce it is a fact the narrator withholds until the final line.

themes.name: Puritan inheritance
themes.summary: Salem, Mather, the meeting-house and the devil in the woods sit under the American stories the way old churches sit under English ones. Irving's schoolmaster reads witchcraft history for entertainment; Hawthorne's characters live in its consequences.
themes.development: What begins as a comic superstition in Irving becomes, in Hawthorne, a religion that can ruin a man in one night.

themes.name: American settings
themes.summary: A Dutch valley, a swamp, a forest, a tarn, a frontier clearing. The settings are local, named and recent, and the supernatural in them belongs to a particular soil, not to old castles.
themes.development: Lovecraft's castle at the end is the one European setting in the book, and even that turns out to be somewhere else.

themes.name: Money and land
themes.summary: Irving's ghost story is also a story about a poor schoolmaster's designs on a rich man's barns, and The Devil and Tom Walker is about usury. The supernatural keeps arriving where property is at stake.
themes.development: The theme fades as the stories move indoors: by Gilman and Freeman the question is authority inside a household, no longer property.

techniques.name: Found manuscripts
techniques.definition: Presenting a tale as something recorded, inherited or overheard.
techniques.inThisBook: Irving attributes Sleepy Hollow to the papers of Diedrich Knickerbocker and ends with a note on a man who told it at a corporation meeting. Bierce uses a coroner's inquest and a dead man's diary. The distance is part of the joke and part of the fright.

techniques.name: Unreliable narrators
techniques.definition: A first-person account the reader is meant to read against.
techniques.inThisBook: Poe's three stories open with a denial of madness and close with a confession. Gilman's narrator is wrong about the paper and right about the marriage, which is the harder version of the same device.

techniques.name: Comedy and horror
techniques.definition: Keeping a light, ironic tone over frightening material.
techniques.inThisBook: Irving spends pages on pies and dancing before anything appears on the road, and describes an heiress in the same breath as her father's poultry. The laughter is what makes the ride home work.

techniques.name: American settings
techniques.definition: Using real, local geography instead of generic gothic scenery.
techniques.inThisBook: The Tappan Zee, Tarry Town, the Dutch burying ground, a Missouri clearing. Each story puts its horror somewhere a reader could drive to.

techniques.name: Symbolic objects
techniques.definition: A single physical thing that carries the whole tale.
techniques.inThisBook: A pumpkin, a veil, a heart, a cat, a boarded window, a pattern on a wall, a mirror. The collection can almost be indexed by its objects.

techniques.name: Withheld endings
techniques.definition: Keeping the decisive piece of information out of the story, or until the final sentence.
techniques.inThisBook: Irving never says what happened to Ichabod; Bierce's Boarded Window holds its explanation to the last line; Hawthorne refuses to say whether the forest meeting was a dream.

techniques.name: American Gothic
techniques.definition: Gothic machinery adapted to a country without ruins.
techniques.inThisBook: No abbeys, no hereditary curses older than the colony. What these writers use instead is recent history — a Revolutionary cavalryman, a witch trial, a frontier cabin — which is why the stories still feel close.

quotations.text: this sequestered glen has long been known by the name of SLEEPY HOLLOW, and its rustic lads are called the Sleepy Hollow Boys throughout all the neighboring country
quotations.context: Introducing the valley, before any character appears.
quotations.analysis: The place is named by its reputation, not on a map, and the capitals make it sound quoted from local speech. Irving establishes that everything in the story is what people say about the place.
quotations.source: 1820 text, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow

quotations.text: A drowsy, dreamy influence seems to hang over the land, and to pervade the very atmosphere.
quotations.context: The next sentence, explaining the valley's character.
quotations.analysis: Two adjectives that mean nearly the same thing, and a verb that will not commit — seems. Irving builds the supernatural out of climate and hearsay, so that nothing in the story ever has to be true.
quotations.source: 1820 text, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow

quotations.text: the apparition of a figure on horseback without a head
quotations.context: The dominant spirit of the place, as the neighbourhood describes it.
quotations.analysis: The most famous image in American folklore is introduced as a piece of village reputation, at second hand, several thousand words before anything rides. Irving lets the community invent the ghost, and then sends Ichabod out to meet what it invented.
quotations.source: 1820 text, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow

quotations.text: He was tall, but exceedingly lank, with narrow shoulders, long arms and legs, hands that dangled a mile out of his sleeves
quotations.context: The first description of Ichabod Crane.
quotations.analysis: Comic exaggeration done with exact parts — shoulders, arms, sleeves — so that the reader can see him before the sentence ends. Irving is teaching American prose how to do caricature without cruelty, and the technique passes straight into Twain.
quotations.source: 1820 text, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow

quotations.text: Spare the rod and spoil the child
quotations.context: Ichabod's professional motto, quoted approvingly by the narrator.
quotations.analysis: A proverb from Proverbs, used to license a schoolmaster's caning and reported with a perfectly straight face. It is the first sign that this narrator will tell you what people believe without ever telling you what he believes.
quotations.source: 1820 text, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow

quotations.text: his appetite for the marvellous, and his powers of digesting it, were equally extraordinary
quotations.context: On Ichabod's reading, which includes Cotton Mather's history of New England witchcraft.
quotations.analysis: The eating metaphor runs through the whole portrait — the man who can out-eat anybody also swallows every story he is told. Irving makes credulity a form of greed, which sets up the ride home exactly.
quotations.source: 1820 text, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow

quotations.text: a huge feeder, and, though lank, had the dilating powers of an anaconda
quotations.analysis: A schoolmaster compared to a snake swallowing something whole, in a sentence that is entirely affectionate. The joke also tells you what he wants from the farm, which is everything on it.
quotations.source: 1820 text, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow

quotations.text: was found the hat of the unfortunate Ichabod, and close beside it a shattered pumpkin
quotations.context: What the search party finds by the brook in the morning.
quotations.analysis: The evidence is laid out and not interpreted: a hat, a pumpkin, hoof-prints at furious speed. Irving gives the reader everything needed to solve it and then spends his last pages letting the village prefer the ghost.
quotations.source: 1820 text, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow

timeline.label: The Revolution ends
timeline.detail: The Hessian trooper of the legend is a soldier of that war, which was within living memory when Irving wrote.

timeline.label: Irving's 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' published
timeline.detail: Published in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent., which made Irving the first American author to live by his pen abroad.

timeline.label: Irving's 'The Devil and Tom Walker' published
timeline.detail: Printed in Tales of a Traveller, moving the same comic-gothic method to New England money.

timeline.label: Hawthorne's 'Young Goodman Brown' published
timeline.detail: Hawthorne, a descendant of a Salem witch-trial judge, publishes the forest story anonymously in a magazine.

timeline.label: Poe's 'The Fall of the House of Usher' published
timeline.detail: Poe in Burton's Gentleman's Magazine, setting the terms for American gothic interiors.

timeline.label: Poe's 'The Tell-Tale Heart' and 'The Black Cat' published
timeline.detail: The Tell-Tale Heart and The Black Cat appear within months of each other.

timeline.label: Bierce's 'The Boarded Window' published
timeline.detail: Bierce, a Civil War veteran, publishes the frontier story whose last line does all the work.

timeline.label: Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 'The Yellow Wall-Paper' published
timeline.detail: Gilman's story of a rest cure appears in The New England Magazine.

timeline.label: Mary Wilkins Freeman's 'The Shadows on the Wall' published
timeline.detail: Mary Wilkins Freeman's New England ghost story, told almost entirely through the household's conversation.

timeline.label: Lovecraft's 'The Outsider' in Weird Tales
timeline.detail: Lovecraft in Weird Tales, closing the century the collection covers.

places.name: Sleepy Hollow, New York
places.note: The Dutch burying ground and the bridge the Horseman must not cross.

places.name: Salem, Massachusetts

criticalViews.position: A holiday canon assembled after the fact
criticalViews.summary: None of these stories was written for Halloween; the association was built by publishers, anthologists and a century of repetition, which the edition's introduction documents.
criticalViews.counter: Readers have been telling ghost stories in the dark half of the year for far longer than the modern holiday has existed, so the fit may be older than the marketing.

criticalViews.summary: The evidence at the brook — a hat, a shattered pumpkin, hoof-prints — points at Brom Bones, and the narrator lets you see it.
criticalViews.counter: The story spends its first thousand words establishing that this valley makes people believe things, and it ends with the village choosing the ghost. The joke is on anyone certain either way.

criticalViews.summary: Lacking abbeys and hereditary curses, these writers use recent history — a Revolutionary soldier, a witch trial, a frontier cabin — which is why the horror feels close to the ground.
criticalViews.counter: Lovecraft's castle and Poe's Usher borrow European machinery wholesale; the American gothic keeps importing what it claims not to need.

essayQuestions.question: How does Irving make a ghost story out of village gossip?
essayQuestions.focus: Hearsay, narration and the withheld fact
plan: Start with the naming of the Hollow and the drowsy influence: reputation before event.
Show the Horseman introduced as something the neighbourhood says, thousands of words before the ride.
Follow Ichabod's credulity as a character trait the plot then uses.
Set the evidence at the brook — hat, pumpkin, hoof-prints — against the village's preferred version.
Conclude on what the story gains by never settling it.

essayQuestions.question: What changes across the century this collection covers?
essayQuestions.focus: From a shared ghost to a private one
plan: Take Irving's communal legend as the starting point.
Move to Hawthorne, where the horror is moral and may be a dream.
Use Poe's confessional narrators as the turn inward.
Show Bierce, Gilman and Freeman removing the explanation altogether.
End on The Outsider, where the narrator does not know what he is.

essayQuestions.question: Why do so many of these stories hide something?
plan: List the hidden things: a face behind crape, a heart under boards, a body in a wall, a boarded window, a figure behind a pattern.
Consider what concealment does to a short story's structure.
Examine how each story reveals — or declines to reveal — in its last lines.
Compare Hawthorne's refusal with Bierce's single closing sentence.
Argue for which method the collection makes most effective.

discussionQuestions: Irving gives you the pumpkin. Do you believe in the Horseman anyway?
Ichabod wants the farm as much as the girl. Does that change how you read his fate?
Poe's narrators insist they are sane. At what point in each story did you stop agreeing?
The Yellow Wall-Paper sits among ghost stories here. Is it one?
None of these was written for Halloween. Does reading them as Halloween stories cost anything?
Which of the twelve would you give someone who says they do not like ghost stories?
